summary: Defines the WebRTC threat model and analyzes the security threats to real-time communication in browsers.

eli5.summary: A list of the ways a video call in a browser could go wrong or be attacked.

questions: what are the security threats in webrtc
what is the webrtc threat model
why does webrtc need user consent for camera access
how does webrtc prevent denial of service attacks
subtitle: What can go wrong when a web page is allowed to place calls from your browser, and what has to be true to keep it safe.

tldr.problem: WebRTC lets a web server tell your browser to open the camera and microphone and send data to other machines. A malicious site could use that to bug you, attack other networks, or intercept your calls.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC starts from the browser security model (the browser protects the user from any site, even a hostile one) and walks through the threats: access to local devices, sending traffic without the receiver's consent, and attacks on call security and privacy.
tldr.outcome: It sets the requirements that the companion RFC 8827 turns into an architecture: consent for device access scoped to an origin, ICE-based consent before traffic is sent, and encrypted media with a key exchange the calling site cannot see.

today: RFC 8826 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it is the threat analysis paired with RFC 8827, which describes the security architecture that addresses it.

sections.title: Why WebRTC Needs a Threat Model
sections.content:
Unlike a conventional SIP-based soft phone, a WebRTC call is directly controlled by a web server. The server's JavaScript calls standardized browser APIs to set up the call, and the same server usually carries the signaling messages between the two browsers. Media then flows directly between the browsers.

That makes malicious calling services a new problem. If a site could make the browser call anyone at any time, it could bug the user's computer by calling a recording service. If the APIs let the server send arbitrary content, they could be used to bypass firewalls or mount denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. The companion document RFC 8827 describes the security architecture that answers these threats.
sections.eli5: In a normal phone, you decide who to call. In a browser call, the website helps decide, so a bad website could try to make your computer call the wrong place.

sections.title: The Browser Threat Model
sections.content:
The starting point is the core browser guarantee: users can safely visit arbitrary web sites and execute scripts provided by those sites. That includes sites hosting malicious scripts, since an attacker can easily divert users there, for example with display advertisements. The browser acts as the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) and runs scripts in a sandbox. The RFC distinguishes Web attackers, who can lure you to their sites but do not control the network, from network attackers, who control your network.

Three existing mechanisms matter. First, browsers strictly limit or forbid a site's access to local resources such as files, the camera and the microphone, and avoid dialogs of the form "click here to bypass security checks" because users tend to consent to them. Second, the same-origin policy (SOP) stops a script from reading responses from a different origin, which prevents one server from attacking another through the user's browser. Third, CORS and WebSockets give controlled escape hatches, and both start with a consent verification handshake. Designing a correct handshake has proved difficult, and WebSockets uses masking to randomize the bits on the wire to resist cross-protocol attacks.
sections.eli5: Your browser is like a careful school guard. Every website gets its own playground and cannot peek into the others. If two playgrounds want to talk, the guard first checks that both sides agree.

sections.title: Consent for Cameras, Microphones and Screens
sections.content:
At minimum, arbitrary sites MUST NOT be able to initiate calls to arbitrary locations without user consent. The hard question is the scope of that consent. The RFC describes two models: you send media to entity A because you want to talk to A, or A asks for your devices while promising to pass the media to B. The browser can only verify and check authorization for whoever controls where the media goes, since A could always forward the media to C.

Two scenarios show the tension. With a dedicated calling service the user may want long-term permission, but that implicitly lets the service bug the computer at will. When calling the site you are on (for example a shopping site's "talk to a representative" window), consent should last only for the call, and the browser chrome must clearly show the call is still going on. Screen sharing is harder still: users may overshare, and a site that shares your screen can briefly open your bank or webmail in a window and read it, which breaks the same-origin invariant. The RFC therefore suggests screen sharing may need a higher level of consent than camera or microphone access.
sections.eli5: Letting a website use your camera is like handing a visitor your house key. You might hand it over for one visit, but you would not want them to keep it forever, and sharing your whole screen is like letting them wander through every room.

sections.title: Scoping Consent to an Origin
sections.content:
Because the basic unit of web sandboxing is the origin, a script from origin A MUST only be allowed to initiate communications, and so reach the camera and microphone, if the user has specifically authorized that origin. Origin alone can be too coarse: once Alice allows a site to make one call, the site can later bug her computer on any future visit, including one induced via a mash-up or ad network.

The RFC lists three countermeasures, none perfect: individual consent (ask for every call, which trains users to click OK), callee-oriented consent (only allow calls to a given user, which a malicious site can subvert by claiming any callee) and cryptographic consent (only allow calls to given keying material or a cryptographically established identity). It also warns that a calling page loaded over HTTP can be hijacked by a network attacker who injects an IFRAME and forged JavaScript, and that untrusted JavaScript included in an HTTPS page runs with that page's authority.
sections.eli5: A permission slip that says "this website may use my camera" is useful, but a bad actor who sneaks onto that website can reuse it. So the slip may also need to name who you are allowed to call.

sections.title: Consent to Receive Traffic
sections.content:
Allowing web applications unrestricted network access would turn the browser into an attack platform against machines behind a firewall or NAT. So the target of the traffic must explicitly consent, and until consent is verified, traffic other than the consent handshake MUST NOT be sent to that endpoint.

The RFC points to ICE (RFC 8445), which already needs a handshake for NAT hole-punching. Because the site starting ICE is presumed malicious, the receiver must show knowledge of a value the site cannot see: the STUN transaction IDs must be generated by the browser and MUST NOT be exposed to the script, even through a diagnostic interface. ICE keepalives are indications and so cannot prove continuing consent; RFC 7675 provides consent freshness. The RFC also records why legacy alternatives (plain STUN checks or RTCP as a reachability check) were judged unsatisfactory, and notes that the working group ultimately decided to require ICE.

Consent verification does not stop a malicious site from using up a user's bandwidth, which is why good congestion control for WebRTC protocols is needed.
sections.eli5: Before the browser sends a big pile of data to some computer, it knocks and waits for that computer to say "yes, I want it". The website is not allowed to fake the answer.

sections.title: Protecting the Call Itself
sections.content:
It MUST be possible to establish a channel secure against both message recovery and message modification, for data and for voice and video. Unlike a SIP proxy, the calling service also controls the application running in the browser, so it can be a threat. The RFC separates two attacks. In a retrospective compromise the service was honest during the call but is hacked later; in a during-call attack it is compromised while the call is under way.

Against the first, a key exchange the service cannot read is required: if keys travel through the service (as with SDES), they are likely to be logged. An automatic public-key exchange is imperative and SHOULD provide Forward Secrecy, and the API MUST NOT let scripts extract long-term keys or stored traffic keys. The second is much harder, because the service can act as a man in the middle. Key continuity, short authentication strings (as in ZRTP) and third-party identity (web identity providers) are each examined. Key continuity and short strings suffer from users clicking through warnings, legitimate key changes across browsers, and voice cloning. Third-party identity binds the user's identity to the keying material and resists active attack by the calling site. The RFC also notes that if the page can view or modify the media, the user does not get the assurance they expect, so a secure media mode where the site verifiably gives up access is needed.
sections.eli5: Locking your messages is not enough if the postman can make the lock himself. The keys must be made by the two people talking, and they need a way to be sure they are talking to the right person.

sections.title: Privacy: IP Addresses and Fingerprints
sections.content:
As soon as a callee sends ICE candidates, the caller learns their IP addresses, and the server-reflexive address reveals a lot about location. Implementations may suppress the start of ICE until the callee answers, and either side may hide its location by forcing all traffic through a TURN server. Sites can also cause the browser to reveal addresses, which can expose the network environment of a user behind a VPN; RFC 8828 covers this.

Persistent identifiers such as reused DTLS certificates and RTCP CNAMEs can link anonymous calls, so browsers need ways to reset them (for example with the same lifetime as cookies) and sites should be able to force fresh identifiers. Every new API also adds browser fingerprinting risk, since the presence or absence of devices can identify a browser. The RFC says the API needs to balance functionality against that risk. It does not try to prevent malicious peers, for example one recording the call or doing prank calling.
sections.eli5: When you phone someone, they might learn roughly where you are. The browser can route the call through a middleman so your address stays secret, and it can use a fresh disguise for each call so nobody can tell it is you again.

viz.caption: WAYS TO CHECK THE OTHER END DURING A CALL (RFC 8826 SECTION 4.3.2)

items.title: Key continuity
items.text: Remember a peer's public key and alarm when it changes. Users get alerts for legitimate changes and learn to click through.

items.title: Short authentication strings
items.text: Compare a string derived from the key exchange, as ZRTP does. Optional, and voice cloning weakens it.

items.title: Third-party identity
items.text: A web identity provider binds a user identity to the keying material, resisting active attack by the calling site.

items.title: Certificates
items.text: PKI-style certificates work in the special case of calls from end users to large sites.
